title: Parity (Even or Odd) of Products, Quotients, and Compositions
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: Assume that f is an even function, g is an odd function, and both f and g are defined on the entire real line (-infinity, infinity). Determine whether each of the following functions (where defined) is even or odd: (a) f*g, (b) f/g, (c) g/f, (d) f^2 = f*f, (e) g^2 = g*g, (f) f o g, (g) g o f, (h) f o f, and (i) g o g.
finalAnswer: \text{(a) Odd},\quad \text{(b) Odd},\quad \text{(c) Odd},\quad \text{(d) Even},\quad \text{(e) Even},\quad \text{(f) Even},\quad \text{(g) Even},\quad \text{(h) Even},\quad \text{(i) Odd}

steps.title: State the Defining Parity Identities for f and g
steps.explanation: By hypothesis, replacing x with -x leaves f(x) unchanged and negates g(x) for all real x.
steps.why: Definitions of even and odd functions on (-infinity, infinity).

steps.title: Test the Algebraic Products and Quotients in Parts (a)-(e)
steps.mathExpression: \begin{aligned} \text{(a) } (fg)(-x) &= f(-x)g(-x) = f(x)(-g(x)) = -(fg)(x) \implies \text{Odd} \\ \text{(b) } (f/g)(-x) &= \frac{f(-x)}{g(-x)} = \frac{f(x)}{-g(x)} = -(f/g)(x) \implies \text{Odd} \\ \text{(c) } (g/f)(-x) &= \frac{g(-x)}{f(-x)} = \frac{-g(x)}{f(x)} = -(g/f)(x) \implies \text{Odd} \\ \text{(d) } f^2(-x) &= (f(-x))^2 = (f(x))^2 = f^2(x) \implies \text{Even} \\ \text{(e) } g^2(-x) &= (g(-x))^2 = (-g(x))^2 = g^2(x) \implies \text{Even} \end{aligned}
steps.explanation: Multiplying or dividing an even function and an odd function introduces a single minus sign, producing an odd function in (a), (b), and (c). Squaring either an even or an odd function squares the sign ((+/-1)^2 = +1), producing an even function in (d) and (e).
steps.why: Pointwise multiplication and division obey sign parity rules: (+)(-) = - (odd) and (-)(-) = + (even).

steps.title: Test the Four Compositions in Parts (f)-(i)
steps.mathExpression: \begin{aligned} \text{(f) } (f \circ g)(-x) &= f(g(-x)) = f(-g(x)) = f(g(x)) = (f \circ g)(x) \implies \text{Even} \\ \text{(g) } (g \circ f)(-x) &= g(f(-x)) = g(f(x)) = (g \circ f)(x) \implies \text{Even} \\ \text{(h) } (f \circ f)(-x) &= f(f(-x)) = f(f(x)) = (f \circ f)(x) \implies \text{Even} \\ \text{(i) } (g \circ g)(-x) &= g(g(-x)) = g(-g(x)) = -g(g(x)) = -(g \circ g)(x) \implies \text{Odd} \end{aligned}
steps.explanation: In (f), the outer even function f absorbs the minus sign from g(-x) = -g(x). In (g) and (h), the inner even function f absorbs the minus sign immediately. Only in (i), where both inner and outer functions are odd, does the minus sign pass through both layers to yield -(g o g)(x).
steps.why: A composition of parity functions is even if at least one component is even, and odd if both components are odd.
